interpretive_safeguards.teraphim: Rachel’s motive remains unstated. Household cult, domestic or ancestral function, divination, and inheritance-related proposals are represented as debated possibilities; no single motive or exact object function is asserted.
interpretive_safeguards.mizpah_and_heap: Galeed/Jegar-sahadutha, pillar and heap are treated as bilingual boundary/witness markers in an oath setting with meal/sacrifice context; Mizpah is not recast as a sentimental friendship blessing.
interpretive_safeguards.wrestling_and_israel: Genesis narrates a man wrestling; Jacob interprets the encounter as seeing God face-to-face. Divine manifestation, messenger, mysterious man, and later reception views remain distinguished. Hosea 12 is reception context only. The Israel name explanation preserves striving/God/human wordplay and lexical uncertainty.
interpretive_safeguards.peniel_and_dietary_note: Peniel/Penuel is tied to Jacob’s face-of-God explanation. The hip/thigh injury receives no modern diagnosis. Genesis 32:32 is treated as an etiological dietary note; later halakhic detail is not read back as fully specified in Genesis.
interpretive_safeguards.reconciliation: Genesis 33’s seven bows are described as diplomatic/kinship prostration without assuming worship; embrace, kiss, and weeping remain the immediate response. The marked “kissed” tradition is not used to prove murderous intent. Gift/“blessing” and face-like-God language are read with Peniel without divinizing Esau.
interpretive_safeguards.dinah_and_shechem: Genesis 34 represents the taking/intercourse/humiliation language as sexual violation; lexical debate is preserved without invented details or euphemistic romance. Shechem’s later attachment does not undo the violation; Jacob’s silence is recorded without invented motive.
interpretive_safeguards.circumcision_and_massacre: The circumcision proposal is treated as deception, not covenant conversion. Third-day killing, Dinah’s rescue, and plunder of property, livestock, women, and children are stated plainly; the text gives no divine command for the massacre and no warrant for later ethnic hostility.
interpretive_safeguards.bethel_purification: Household gods and earrings are handled in their narrative context; earrings are not intrinsically labeled idolatrous. Purification and garment change, burial under the tree, terror of God, altar/pillar/libation/oil, and Bethel’s sacred setting are treated without inventing events.
interpretive_safeguards.family_transition: Rachel’s labor, Ben-oni/Benjamin, death and burial location traditions remain geographically qualified; no modern tomb is declared certain. Reuben/Bilhah is recorded as a household and power episode, with Genesis 49 as context only. Twelve sons frame the tribal transition; Isaac’s death and joint burial by Esau and Jacob are included.
interpretive_safeguards.edom_genealogy_and_politics: Genesis 36 functions as family record and clan/territorial/political ethnography. Alluf is qualified as chief/leader; Horite identity is not racialized. Edomite place identifications have confidence limits and no invented coordinates. Anah’s yemim remains lexically uncertain.
interpretive_safeguards.genesis_36_31: The Edomite kings list and “before any king reigned over the Israelites” comparison raise chronological/compositional questions. Multiple readings are represented; the verse alone does not date all Genesis.
interpretive_safeguards.archaeology: Comparative archaeological and historical material contextualizes cultural and political patterns but is not presented as proof of Jacob, Laban, Dinah, Shechem’s prince, or specific patriarchal events.
interpretive_safeguards.divine_messenger: Genesis 31, 32, and 35 divine/messenger material is described from text and Hebrew/worldview context; a divine-council model is not forced onto every scene.
